title: GMAT Focus Scores: 205–805 and How to Play the Test
summary: How the new 205–805 scale works, why every section counts equally, and the pacing + review strategy that follows.

nodes.label: Three equal sections
nodes.note: Quant, Verbal, Data Insights all count

nodes.label: Adaptive + review
nodes.note: Steady accuracy; edit up to 3 per section

chunks.heading: A new scale — don't compare to the old 800
chunks.body: GMAT Focus totals run **205–805 in 10-point steps**, built from **all three sections equally**. Crucially, **a Focus score is NOT the same as an old-GMAT score** — a 645 Focus is a very different percentile from a 645 on the old 200–800 scale, so **compare using percentiles, not raw numbers**.
chunks.realExample: Someone quoting '650 is average' from old GMAT advice is misleading you — on Focus, look up what percentile your target total sits at, because the scale and distribution changed.
chunks.memoryHook: 205–805 is a NEW scale. Judge by percentile, never by old-GMAT numbers.

chunks.heading: Every section counts — balance wins
chunks.body: Because **Quant, Verbal and Data Insights are equally weighted**, a lopsided profile hurts more than before. **Data Insights is now a full third**, so the old habit of coasting through Integrated Reasoning is a costly mistake.
chunks.realExample: A strong-Quant, weak-DI candidate who ignored Data Insights can score lower overall than a balanced candidate — the third that used to barely count now counts fully.
chunks.memoryHook: Three equal thirds. A weak section (especially DI) drags the whole total.

chunks.heading: Adaptive: accuracy beats speed-guessing
chunks.body: Each section is **computer-adaptive**, adjusting difficulty to your answers. Careless early errors can lower your difficulty path, but **rushing to finish blindly is worse** — aim for **steady accuracy** and use the timer as a guide, not a whip.
chunks.realExample: Getting three easy questions wrong by rushing hurts more than spending your time and missing one hard one — the adaptive engine rewards consistent correctness.
chunks.memoryHook: Adaptive rewards steady accuracy. Don't trade easy points for speed.

chunks.heading: Use the review & edit safety net
chunks.body: You can **bookmark and change up to three answers per section**. Bank an answer for every question, **flag the ones you're unsure of**, and if time remains, revisit up to three. Never leave a question blank — the adaptive test needs an answer to move on.
chunks.realExample: Finish a section with four minutes left? Reopen your two bookmarked coin-flips on the review screen and give them a second, calmer look — that's points the old GMAT never let you reclaim.
chunks.memoryHook: Answer all, bookmark doubts, edit up to 3. A blank is a wasted safety net.

recall.q: What is the GMAT Focus total score range and step size?
recall.a: 205 to 805, in 10-point increments, from three equally-weighted sections.

recall.q: Why can't you compare a GMAT Focus score to an old GMAT score directly?
recall.a: It's a new scale with a different distribution, so you should compare using percentiles, not raw numbers.

recall.q: Why does Data Insights matter more now?
recall.a: It's equally weighted with Quant and Verbal — a full third of the total — not a minor add-on.

recall.q: What does the adaptive format reward?
recall.a: Steady accuracy — rushing and making careless early errors hurts more than spending time on fewer questions.

recall.q: How does the review-and-edit feature work?
recall.a: You can bookmark questions and change up to three answers per section before time expires.
